{{Short description|Point and its four nearest neighbors}}
[[File:Five point stencil illustration.png|right|thumb|An illustration of the five-point stencil in one and two dimensions (top, and bottom, respectively).]]
In [[numerical analysis]], given a [[square grid]] in one or two dimensions, the '''five-point stencil''' of a point in the grid is a [[stencil (numerical analysis)|stencil]] made up of the point itself together with its four "neighbors". It is used to write [[finite difference]] approximations to [[derivative]]s at grid points. It is an example of [[numerical differentiation]].

==In one dimension==
In one dimension, if the spacing between points in the grid is ''h'', then the five-point stencil of a point ''x'' in the grid is
:<math display="block"> \{x-2h, x-h, x, x+h, x+2h\}.</math>

===1D first derivative===
The first derivative of a [[function (mathematics)|function]] ''f'' of a [[real number|real]] variable at a point ''x'' can be approximated using a five-point stencil as:<ref>{{cite book |title=Numerical Analysis |last=Sauer |first=Timothy |publisher=Pearson |year=2012 |isbn=978-0-321-78367-7 |pages=250}}</ref>
:<math display="block">f'(x) \approx \frac{-f(x+2 h)+8 f(x+h)-8 f(x-h)+f(x-2h)}{12 h}</math>

The center point ''f''(''x'') itself is not involved, only the four neighboring points.

====Derivation====
This formula can be obtained by writing out the four [[Taylor series]] of <math>f(x \pm h)</math> and <math>f(x \pm 2h)</math> at the point <math>a</math>, up to terms of ''h''<sup>3</sup> (or up to terms of ''h''<sup>5</sup> to get an error estimation as well), evaluating each series at <math>a = x \mp h</math> and <math>a = x \mp 2h</math> respectively (to get everything in common terms of <math>f^{(k)}(x)</math>), and solving this system of four equations to get ''f''&thinsp;&prime;(''x''). Actually, we have at points ''x''&nbsp;+&nbsp;''h'' and ''x''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;''h'':
:<math display="block">f(x \pm h) = f(x) \pm h f'(x) + \frac{h^2}{2}f''(x) \pm \frac{h^3}{6} f^{(3)}(x) + O_{1\pm}(h^4). \qquad (E_{1\pm}).</math>

Evaluating <math>(E_{1+})-(E_{1-})</math> gives us
:<math display="block">f(x+h) - f(x-h) = 2hf'(x) + \frac{h^3}{3}f^{(3)}(x) + O_1(h^4). \qquad (E_1).</math>

The residual term O<sub>1</sub>(''h''<sup>4</sup>) should be of the order of ''h''<sup>5</sup> instead of ''h''<sup>4</sup> because if the terms of ''h''<sup>4</sup> had been written out in (''E''<sub>1+</sub>) and (''E''<sub>1&minus;</sub>), it can be seen that they would have canceled each other out by {{math|''f''(''x'' + ''h'') − ''f''(''x'' − ''h'')}}. But for this calculation, it is left like that since the order of error estimation is not treated here (cf below).

Similarly, we have
:<math display="block">f(x \pm 2h) = f(x) \pm 2h f'(x) + \frac{4h^2}{2!} f''(x) \pm \frac{8h^3}{3!} f^{(3)}(x) + O_{2\pm}(h^4). \qquad (E_{2\pm})</math>
and <math>(E_{2+}) - (E_{2-})</math> gives us
:<math display="block">f(x+2h) - f(x-2h) = 4hf'(x) + \frac{8h^3}{3}f^{(3)}(x) + O_2(h^5). \qquad (E_2).</math>

In order to eliminate the terms of ''&fnof;''<sup>(3)</sup>(''x''), calculate 8&nbsp;×&nbsp;(''E''<sub>1</sub>)&nbsp;−&nbsp;(''E''<sub>2</sub>)
:<math display="block">8f(x+h) - 8f(x-h) - f(x+2h) + f(x-2h) = 12h f'(x) + O(h^5)</math>
thus giving the formula as above. Note: the coefficients of f in this formula, (8, -8,-1,1), represent a specific example of the more general [[Savitzky–Golay filter]].

====Error estimate====
The error in this approximation is of [[Landau notation|order]] ''h''<sup>&nbsp;4</sup>. That can be seen from the expansion<ref name="as252">Abramowitz & Stegun, Table 25.2</ref>
:<math display="block"> \frac{-f(x+2 h)+8 f(x+h)-8 f(x-h)+f(x-2h)}{12 h}=f'(x)-\frac{1}{30} f^{(5)}(x) h^4+O(h^5)</math>
which can be obtained by expanding the left-hand side in a [[Taylor series]]. Alternatively, apply [[Richardson extrapolation]] to the [[central difference]] approximation to <math>f'(x)</math> on grids with spacing 2''h'' and ''h''.

===1D higher-order derivatives===
The centered difference formulas for five-point stencils approximating second, third, and fourth derivatives are
:<math display="block"> \begin{align}
  f''(x)     &\approx \frac{-f(x+2 h)+16 f(x+h)-30 f(x) + 16 f(x-h) - f(x-2h)}{12 h^2}
 \\[1ex]
 f^{(3)}(x) &\approx \frac{f(x+2 h)-2 f(x+h) + 2 f(x-h) - f(x-2h)}{2 h^3}
 \\[1ex]
  f^{(4)}(x) &\approx \frac{f(x+2 h)-4 f(x+h)+6 f(x) - 4 f(x-h) + f(x-2h)}{h^4}
\end{align} </math>

The errors in these approximations are ''O''(''h''{{i sup|4}}), ''O''(''h''{{i sup|2}}) and ''O''(''h''{{i sup|2}}) respectively.<ref name="as252"/>

===Relationship to Lagrange interpolating polynomials===
As an alternative to deriving the finite difference weights from the Taylor series, they may be obtained by differentiating the [[Lagrange polynomial]]s
:<math display="block">\ell_j(\xi) = \prod_{i=0,\, i\neq j}^{k} \frac{\xi-x_i}{x_j-x_i}, </math>
where the interpolation points are
:<math display="block">
x_0 = x-2h,\quad x_1 = x-h,\quad x_2 = x,\quad x_3 = x+h,\quad x_4 = x+2h.
</math>

Then, the quartic polynomial <math>p_4(x)</math> interpolating {{math|''f''(''x'')}} at these five points is
:<math display="block"> p_4(x) = \sum_{j=0}^4 f(x_j) \ell_j(x) </math>
and its derivative is
:<math display="block"> p_4'(x) = \sum_{j=0}^4 f(x_j) \ell'_j(x). </math>

So, the finite difference approximation of {{math|''f''&thinsp;&prime;(''x'')}} at the middle point {{math|1=''x'' = ''x''<sub>2</sub>}} is
:<math display="block">
f'(x_2) = \ell_0'(x_2) f(x_0) + \ell_1'(x_2) f(x_1) + \ell_2'(x_2) f(x_2)  + \ell_3'(x_2) f(x_3) + \ell_4'(x_2) f(x_4) + O(h^4)
</math>

Evaluating the derivatives of the five Lagrange polynomials at {{math|1=''x'' = ''x''<sub>2</sub>}} gives the same weights as above. This method can be more flexible as the extension to a non-uniform grid is quite straightforward.

==In two dimensions==
In two dimensions, if for example the size of the squares in the grid is ''h'' by ''h'', the five point stencil of a point (''x'',&nbsp;''y'') in the grid is
:<math display="block">\{(x-h, y), (x, y), (x+h, y), (x, y-h), (x, y+h)\}, </math>
forming a pattern that is also called a [[quincunx]]. This stencil is often used to approximate the [[Laplacian]] of a function of two variables:
:<math display="block"> \nabla^2 f(x,y) \approx \frac{f(x-h,y) + f(x+h,y) + f(x,y-h) + f(x,y+h) - 4f(x,y)}{h^2}. </math>

The error in this approximation is ''O''(''h''<sup>&nbsp;2</sup>),<ref>Abramowitz & Stegun, 25.3.30</ref> which may be explained as follows:

From the 3 point stencils for the second derivative of a function with respect to x and y:
:<math display="block">\begin{align}
\frac{\partial ^2 f}{\partial x^2} &=
\frac{f\left(x + \Delta x,y\right) + f\left(x - \Delta x,y\right) - 2f(x,y)}{\Delta x^2} - 2\frac{f^{(4)}(x,y)}{4!} \Delta x^2 + \cdots \\[1ex]
\frac{\partial ^2 f}{\partial y^2} &=
\frac{f\left(x, y + \Delta y\right) + f\left(x, y - \Delta y\right) - 2f(x,y)}{\Delta y^2} - 2\frac{f^{(4)}(x,y)}{4!} \Delta y^2 + \cdots
\end{align}</math>

If we assume <math>\Delta x = \Delta y = h</math>:
:<math display="block">\begin{align}
\nabla^2 f &= \frac{\partial ^2 f}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial ^2 f}{\partial y^2} \\[1ex]
 &= \frac{f\left(x + h,y\right) + f\left(x - h,y\right) + f\left(x, y + h\right) + f\left(x, y - h\right) - 4f(x,y)}{h^2} - 4 \frac{f^{(4)}(x,y)}{4!}h^2 + \cdots \\[1ex]
 &= \frac{f\left(x + h,y\right) + f\left(x - h,y\right) + f\left(x, y + h\right) + f\left(x, y - h\right) - 4f(x,y)}{h^2} + O\left(h^2\right)\\
\end{align}</math>
